passage: Pankaj followed Coach Bhupen's every word and lived for his nod. When he was benched for the semi-final, he burned. He told a teammate the coach obviously preferred others and nearly quit that night. In the morning he asked, "What should I fix to get back in?" Bhupen said, "Your footwork against the short ball, and your temper." Pankaj trained on it. Loving the coach's words, he had also started to ask why behind each one. Meanwhile a senior, Rohit, was using Pankaj's scorebook analysis for a school competition while promising to introduce him to a scout. Weeks passed and nothing came. Pankaj noticed the imbalance. "What exactly will you do with my sheets, and when?" he asked. Rohit dodged, so Pankaj went to the maths teacher, who knew a real analyst, and asked for advice there too. In the nets, Baljeet, a Class 6 boy, copied Pankaj's hairstyle and the way he tapped his bat. Pankaj grinned, then said, "I dropped a catch last week. Don't copy that part. Find your own style."

qa.q: What did Pankaj ask Coach Bhupen after being benched?
qa.a: He asked what he should fix to get back in.

qa.q: How did Pankaj's response to being benched differ from his handling of Rohit's promises?
qa.a: After being benched he nearly quit, then asked the coach what to fix and trained on it; with Rohit he noticed the imbalance, asked clear questions and sought another mentor.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when he was benched for the semi-final?
qa.a: He felt resentful and hurt, believing the coach preferred others.

qa.q: What could Pankaj keep doing for Baljeet?
qa.a: He could keep admitting his own flaws and encouraging Baljeet to find his own style, instead of enjoying the copying.

grounding: A teen athlete's relationships with a coach and a senior show devotion, resentment at being benched, exploitation by a mentor and being idolised by a younger boy.
